title: Ninety Minutes of Resistance Training a Week Could Add Years to Your Life. South Asians Are Doing the Least.
excerpt: A Harvard-led study of 200,000 health professionals found the longevity sweet spot for weight training. The diaspora's cultural preference for cardio over iron may be costing it dearly.
body:
The numbers are in, and they come with a quiet rebuke for anyone who thinks a daily walk is enough.

A study published last week in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, led by researchers at the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, tracked more than 200,000 health professionals over decades and found that people who performed between 90 and 119 minutes of resistance training each week had a 13 per cent lower death rate from any cause compared to those who did none.

Even half an hour a week made a measurable difference. But beyond 120 minutes, the additional benefits flatlined. The longevity curve, it turns out, has a ceiling — and it is lower than most gym culture would suggest.

"Importantly, 90 to 120 minutes per week should not be interpreted as a strict target or threshold," said Yiwen Zhang, the paper's lead author and a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard. "Future research is needed to refine these recommendations."

The study did not examine the type of resistance training in detail — whether participants used barbells, machines, or bodyweight exercises. What mattered was consistency over time.

The Cardio Trap

The finding arrives at a moment when the global health establishment is recalibrating its advice. Both the World Health Organization and the US Department of Health and Human Services already recommend at least two sessions of muscle-strengthening activity per week alongside 150 minutes of cardio. But compliance remains dismal, especially among South Asian populations.

A 2022 study by Zachary Pope, an assistant professor at the University of Oklahoma, found that combining strength training with aerobic activity produced a 40 per cent lower risk of death compared to no exercise at all. The message is unambiguous: cardio alone is not enough.

"If I had to recommend a minimum effective dose, I would say no less than one hour per week of aerobic physical activity combined with muscle strengthening exercises at least two times per week," Pope said.

Why South Asians Should Pay Attention

The diaspora's relationship with resistance training is complicated by culture and habit. Walking remains the dominant form of exercise among older South Asians. Yoga, while valuable for flexibility and mental health, does not load the musculoskeletal system the way progressive resistance does.

The consequences are measurable. South Asians have among the highest rates of sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength — partly driven by lower baseline muscle mass, vegetarian diets that can be protein-insufficient, and a genetic predisposition to visceral fat accumulation. Type 2 diabetes, which affects South Asians at rates two to four times higher than white populations, is directly linked to low muscle mass and poor glucose metabolism.

Resistance training is one of the few interventions that attacks both problems simultaneously. Weight lifting is known to increase glucose uptake in muscle cells, improve insulin sensitivity, and boost bone density — all of which decline faster in South Asian bodies than in most other populations.

"Resistance training is not about bodybuilding, appearance, or achieving a certain physique," said Heather Hunt, a certified strength and conditioning specialist. "It is about preserving the ability to live life on your own terms."

The Independence Equation

For NRIs watching parents age in India or managing their own health in their 40s and 50s, the study reframes the conversation. Falls are the leading cause of injury-related death among older adults globally. Grip strength — a marker of overall muscular fitness — predicts cardiovascular mortality more reliably than blood pressure in several large studies.

The barrier to entry is lower than most people think. A set of resistance bands, a pair of dumbbells, or even bodyweight exercises like squats, planks, and push-ups are sufficient to get started.

"Start small. You can start in your home," Pope recommended. "Muscle strengthening activities are for everyone."

Jess Gorzelitz, an assistant professor at the University of Iowa who studies exercise interventions, put it more bluntly: "Even if it is one workout a month, once a week, a couple minutes while you are waiting to pick your kids up from daycare — the evidence is very clear that something is better than nothing."

What This Means for the Diaspora

The Indian fitness industry is booming, with gym chains and strength training studios expanding across metros. But for the diaspora, the cultural shift has been slower. Community WhatsApp groups still swap walking step counts. Uncles still insist that morning walks and pranayama are sufficient.

They are not. The data now says so explicitly. Ninety minutes a week. Two hours at most. The prescription is not extreme. But ignoring it might be.
